claims.text: Inducing stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations in tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys will improve radiation tolerance.
Stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations can preserve high strength and tensile ductility in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys.
The baseline is a conventionally processed tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy without optimized coherent nanoprecipitation.
A tailored heat-treatment route can generate stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations in the alloy.
Ar+, He+, and D+ ion exposure is relevant to evaluating refractory high-entropy alloys for plasma-facing fusion applications.
The SCCP radiation-tolerance effect should persist from ambient temperature to approximately 1100 °C.
The treatment will produce coherent nanoprecipitates that are uniformly distributed and well bonded to the matrix.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces act as sinks for irradiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.
Defect absorption at coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces reduces irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
Coherent SCCP interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission and relieve stress concentrations that could cause premature cracking.
The SCCP-treated alloy will have lower irradiation-induced defect density than the untreated baseline.
The SCCP-treated alloy will exhibit reduced deuterium retention and fewer defect clusters than the untreated baseline.
Reduced deuterium retention is evidence of reduced irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
Under irradiation, the SCCP-treated alloy will maintain or improve an ultrahigh strength of approximately 2 GPa and tensile ductility above 10%.
An Ar+ fluence of approximately 2.4 × 10^20 at/m^2 is within the reported irradiation range for tungsten-containing refractory high-entropy alloys considered for fusion applications.
The quantitative radiation-tolerance improvement and its response to complex radiation spectra may vary across fusion-reactor conditions.
A controlled comparison can test SCCP-treated and conventionally processed alloys under identical Ar+, He+, and D+ irradiation conditions.
Failure to significantly reduce defect density and deuterium retention, or significant degradation of mechanical properties, would falsify the hypothesis.
